title: Hiddengrid Episode 044: Maria Mercurial session 6, Tower Play

excerpt.verification: A 2026-07-26 fetch returned 127266240 bytes matching the digest recorded at B01: a 128 kbit/s CBR MP3, 16 kHz, nominally stereo, lasting 7954.009 s. Reproduce with `uv run python scripts/fetch_benchmark_media.py hiddengrid-swc-ep044-tower-play`. The window was kept at 0-600000 ms after measurement rather than by default: theme music occupies only 0:03-0:57, the recap ends at 1:50, and the remaining 82% of the window is live play. The episode post is dated 2013-11-29; the media file's own Last-Modified is 2014-05-24, so the published audio was uploaded or replaced months after the post. Re-check the post date without trusting this record: `curl -s <landing_url> | grep -o '<time[^>]*datetime="[^"]*"'` returned `datetime="2013-11-29T20:00:50-05:00"` on 2026-07-26, and the neighbouring episode 043 post is dated a week earlier, consistent with the weekly cadence. The 140524 in the media filename matches the file's Last-Modified, not the post.

recording_conditions.observations: Measured from the file: one mixed track (the two channels differ by 34 dB, so there is no per-speaker channel to diarize from), 16 kHz sampling, so nothing survives above 8 kHz and energy above 7 kHz sits 26 dB down; integrated loudness -19.2 LUFS, 8.2 LU range, true peak +0.2 dBFS, so the audio was levelled and limited in post. Gaps between utterances fall to near-digital silence (1.05% of samples in the window are exactly zero, 4.6% below -78 dBFS), which an open microphone in a shared room does not produce; this is gated or noise-suppressed per speaker. That rules out a raw single-room capture but does not by itself prove remote play: the remote reading rests on the publisher's online-play format, players referred to by handle, and one player being 'AFK' at 00:17:00. Whether the endpoints were also recorded separately before mixdown cannot be determined from the published file. Seven distinct first-person speaking roles are heard inside the window: the game master and the players of Kat, Pulse, James, Grey, Freya and Gartog. How many people hold those roles is a different question, and the audio barely answers it. Exchanges where two roles speak in immediate succession establish those two as different people - Kat with Pulse at 00:02:35, Kat with James at 00:04:04, James with Grey at 00:04:10, Freya with the game master at 00:05:51 - but no three of these roles are ever established as pairwise distinct, and constraints of that shape can all be satisfied by two people (Freya, Grey and Kat one person; the game master, James and Pulse the other). The demonstrated floor is therefore 2. An earlier draft of this manifest claimed 5, which counted roles appearing in the pair evidence rather than people the evidence separates; the goal validator caught it. Raising the floor needs overlapping speech or voice-print separation, neither of which was performed. Read 7 as roles heard and 2 as what this recording proves; the true count is very probably 6 or 7, and that is inference from the publisher's cast and the content, not measurement. Music: the theme song runs 00:00:03-00:00:57 and the host's welcome starts at 00:00:28 over it, so the first 29 s of speech in the window is mixed with music. Overlap is rated medium from laughter and interjections over the recap (00:01:10-00:01:49 carries no detectable pause) rather than from sustained cross-talk.

truth.method: Machine-assisted listen-through on 2026-07-26, not a human ear. The window was decoded twice by different implementations and model families - whisper.cpp large-v3-turbo (beam 5) and openai-whisper medium.en - both run locally on the private copy, and structure was measured with ffmpeg silence, loudness and spectral analysis rather than by any model. A target was verified only where both decodes carry it and a timestamp locates it; where they disagree, the disagreement is stated in the evidence instead of being resolved by guesswork. Contested passages were re-decoded by four more local models (whisper base.en, ggml small.en, ggml small multilingual, and large-v3-turbo at beam 8) and the split reported rather than voted away. Proper-noun spellings that no decode can settle are flagged as such, and two - Entei and nuyen - take their spelling from the publisher's episode tags and Shadowrun setting vocabulary respectively, with the audio only establishing that the word is spoken. This provenance matters for scoring: see benchmarks/notes/hiddengrid-swc-ep044-tower-play.md for what this item can and cannot diagnose, including the engines it must not be used to score without declaring the dependency. Updated 2026-07-26 at B03 with two sources the original pass did not have. A human listener went through the excerpt and reported on four open questions. A target's basis becomes audio_observed because a person heard the target, which is what that value means - not because the ear resolved every question about it. The ear does two things here and neither is settling a spelling: it confirms that a name is present and spoken at the anchor, and it eliminates alternatives that differ in sound, as 'Greg' does from Grey and as 'Garth' does from Gartog. It cannot separate Kat from Cat or Gray from Grey at all, because those differ only in writing. Each item's evidence says which part came from the ear and which from a document. And the publisher's own cast page (https://www.hiddengrid.com/cast-of-shadows/shadowrunners/, read 2026-07-26) lists the player characters by name, which settles spellings no listening could: Kat over Cat, Grey over Gray, Gartog over Gartok, and corroborates James and Pulse. Two of the four questions B02 raised were homophone pairs and were therefore unanswerable by ear - asking a listener to decide Kat against Cat was our error, not theirs, since audio carries no orthography. Freya is not on that cast page, so that spelling still rests on decoder agreement alone and is the one label here with no written source behind it. Updated again 2026-07-26 at B04, on two carried-forward points and nothing else. First, a second human listening of 00:01:55-00:02:26 is now recorded as its own provisional target for the contested 00:02:08 token, marked audio_observed and marked primed, since the listener was told the hypothesis before listening. Primed evidence is real evidence and it is weaker evidence, and the corpus keeps both facts in the item rather than resolving them. Second, the Freya spelling's lack of a written source moved from this field into that item's own evidence, because a scorer reads the item. No other target, measurement or determination here was reopened.

important_entities.label: Jacob
important_entities.evidence: A player is addressed by first name at 00:01:09, 'Jacob, you stole my line', after another player takes his joke. Both decodes agree on the name. It is not among the handles the publisher tags on this episode, and the spelling cannot be settled by ear.

important_entities.label: Entei
important_entities.evidence: At 00:03:42 a player says he will phone 'Ante's character, James', naming the person at the table and the character separately in one breath. Both decodes render the handle as 'Ante'; the publisher tags this episode Entei, which fixes the spelling of a name the audio alone leaves open.

important_entities.label: The game master, credited by the publisher as nulloperations
important_entities.evidence: One voice opens the episode at 00:00:28 with 'welcome to another episode', sets every scene, adjudicates every test, and at 00:06:05 says 'as the game master, I'm not doing rituals' (one decode hears 'aim master'). The role is observed in the audio; the credit is the publisher's.

important_entities.label: Kat
important_entities.evidence: Named in the phone call at 00:04:12 and again at 00:07:08 when the game master moves 'Kat and Pulse' to the building. A human listener reports hearing 'It's Cat' at 00:04:12, which confirms the word but cannot settle the spelling: Kat and Cat are homophones, so no amount of listening decides between them. The publisher's own cast page (https://www.hiddengrid.com/cast-of-shadows/shadowrunners/, read 2026-07-26) does decide it, listing 'Katherine (Kat) - Hunting her clone'. The label was already Kat; it now rests on a written source instead of on a decoder's preference.

important_entities.label: Pulse
important_entities.evidence: The game master places 'Kat and Pulse' outside the building at 00:07:08. The same player says at 00:01:55 that he is going to hit the tower with Kat driving, which ties the name to the plan formed earlier in the window. The spelling is corroborated in writing by the publisher's own cast page (https://www.hiddengrid.com/cast-of-shadows/shadowrunners/, read 2026-07-26), which lists 'Pulse - In prison'.

important_entities.label: James
important_entities.evidence: Introduced at 00:03:42 as Entei's character and addressed in the in-fiction phone call at 00:04:04, 'Hey, James, where the hell are you guys?'. Both decodes agree. The spelling is corroborated in writing by the publisher's own cast page (https://www.hiddengrid.com/cast-of-shadows/shadowrunners/, read 2026-07-26), which lists 'James - Off in Germany with a special mask'.

important_entities.label: Grey
important_entities.evidence: The character who hired the team, reached through James at 00:04:29 and whose apartment the group gathers in at 00:08:16. Two corrections land on this item. A human listener reports Gray or Grey by ear at 00:04:29, which eliminates the 'Greg' one decoder produced. The spelling is then settled in writing rather than by ear, because Gray and Grey are homophones and audio carries no orthography: the publisher's own cast page (https://www.hiddengrid.com/cast-of-shadows/shadowrunners/, read 2026-07-26) lists the retired player character as 'Brother Shango / Mr Grey'. B02 recorded this label as 'Gray'; it was wrong.

important_entities.label: Freya
important_entities.evidence: At 00:05:31 a player narrates Freya in the other room taking aspirin for the headache the ritual left her, then claims the stun damage in the first person at 00:05:46. The spelling has no written source behind it, and it is the only label in this item that does not. Kat, Grey, Gartog, James and Pulse are all on the publisher's cast page (https://www.hiddengrid.com/cast-of-shadows/shadowrunners/, read 2026-07-26); Freya is not, so 'Freya' rests on decoder agreement alone and could as easily be Freyja or Freia. The audio establishes that the name is spoken and roughly how it sounds. Nothing establishes how it is written, and a scoring run that penalises a variant spelling here is measuring a question this item cannot pose.

important_entities.label: Gartog
important_entities.evidence: At 00:08:46 a player takes Gartog into a spare bedroom to swap the cyberdeck cases. Every decoder produced a different name - Gartog, Gartok, Garntak, Garth. A human listener reports 'Gartog' by ear, which eliminates Garth and Garntak but not Gartok, a final-consonant distinction the ear did not separate. The publisher's own cast page (https://www.hiddengrid.com/cast-of-shadows/shadowrunners/, read 2026-07-26) closes that pair: it lists 'Gartog - Working as Roadee for Maria Mercurial'. Name and spelling are now both settled, by ear and in writing respectively.

important_entities.label: The dragon holding the kidnapped target
important_entities.evidence: At 00:00:53 a player summarises the situation as a pop princess 'kidnapped by a dragon'. The antagonist is never given a name inside the window, and this mention sits inside the recap, so it is knowledge stated here about events that happened earlier.

important_entities.label: The tower
important_entities.evidence: The objective the session's plan is built around: 'I'm going to hit the tower' at 00:02:04, after the recap places a tower in the vision the ritual produced.

important_entities.label: The factory
important_entities.evidence: The location already searched, at 00:02:15, 'it took me all day to search the factory'. It is what the group is done with, and it bounds what they still have to do.

important_entities.label: Stuffer Shack
important_entities.evidence: The game master asks at 00:09:46 whether the character can drive to the nearby Stuffer Shack for a repair kit. Neither decode produced the setting's form, offering 'stuffer shack' and 'Steffer Shack', so this probes Shadowrun vocabulary rather than plain transcription.

important_entities.label: nuyen
important_entities.evidence: The fee under discussion at 00:02:50 is 2,500 nuyen. Both decodes wrote 'new yen'. The audio establishes the spoken word and the amount; the spelling is the Shadowrun setting's. A target whose correct form neither engine produced is worth more than one they both got right.

important_events.label: The episode opens with the theme song, and the host's welcome begins over the music.
important_events.evidence: Continuous non-silent audio from 00:00:03 to 00:00:57 by silence detection at -40 dB; the welcome starts at 00:00:28, so speech and music overlap for about 29 s. None of this is campaign content, and a chronicle that reports it as such has misread the episode's furniture for its story.

important_events.label: The game master recaps the previous session: the team's protection target, a kidnapped pop star, is held by a dragon, and a ritual produced a vision of a desolate area with a big-box building and a tower.
important_events.evidence: Game master narration from 00:00:36 to 00:01:50, with players interjecting. These events happened before the window. The recap is the only place the window states them, so a system must attribute them as recalled rather than as occurring here.

important_events.label: Pulse decides to hit the tower that night rather than wait for morning, and Kat agrees to drive him.
important_events.evidence: From 00:01:55 to 00:02:26: 'go sleep and then I'm going to hit the tower', then 'Kat's going to drive me', then 'Screw it, then I'm going to go during the night'. This is the decision the session turns on, and it is made inside the window. A human listener reports hearing 'Cat's gonna drive me', which both decoders place at 00:02:05-00:02:06, so the phrase is now confirmed by ear as well as by machine. One inference sits inside that: the listener was asked about 00:02:08 and reported this sentence, so identifying it as the 00:02:05 line rests on the wording matching verbatim rather than on them naming a timestamp. It is the reading that fits, not a reading they confirmed.

important_events.label: At 00:02:08, in the same breath as the decision to go that night, the protection target is said to be safe in the meantime.
important_events.evidence: A human listener played 00:01:55-00:02:26 and reports 'nothing's going to happen to Maria in the meantime'. That is a person hearing it, which is what audio_observed means, and it is the only support the Maria reading has ever had: six decodes split four to two for 'nothing happens to me'. It is also primed evidence. The listener had been told the suspicion before listening, and B02's own record shows what that does - asked about this same token once before, and knowing the hypothesis, he reported a sentence from two seconds earlier instead. A report obtained after the answer was suggested cannot be weighed as an independent one, so the status stays provisional rather than verified: the ear is now on the record for Maria, and the record says under what conditions. Deciding it needs a fresh listener given the span and not the hypothesis. The priming is stated here, in the item, rather than in a note, because whoever scores against this item is reading this field and not the notes.

important_events.label: Pulse and Kat telephone James, who relays the request to Grey; Grey has James pass on the address and the pair drive over.
important_events.evidence: From 00:03:36 to 00:05:20. The exchange runs through a character relaying a call to another character in the same room, so speaker attribution and character attribution come apart here more sharply than anywhere else in the window.

important_events.label: Freya recovers stun damage from the ritual; the game master grants an in-fiction hour and calls for Body plus Willpower tests.
important_events.evidence: From 00:05:31 to 00:07:05, including 'body plus willpower, your hits reduce your stun damage'. Table mechanics that a chronicle should recognise as rules talk rather than as story.

important_events.label: Gartog starts transplanting the good cyberdeck into the shell of the old case; with no electronics kit on hand the game master sets the attempt at a -2 modifier.
important_events.evidence: From 00:08:46 to 00:09:53: the case swap is described, the game master asks for an electronics build-repair kit, the player has none, and the penalty is set. The attempt itself is resolved after the window ends.

truth.notes: The surname Mercurial appears in no decode of this window; the full name is first spoken at about 00:21:42, well outside it. Inside the window the kidnapped target is 'our pop princess' and 'she'. That makes the episode's title entity a negative control, and B04 narrowed what the control covers rather than leaving the earlier wording standing. The control is now precisely this: 'Mercurial' is not in the window, so an analysis reporting the full name 'Maria Mercurial' from this window is drawing on metadata or on prior sessions and should be scored as an unsupported claim unless it says where the name came from. The first name is a separate question and is no longer flatly absent. The 00:02:08 token is still not settled, but it is no longer unheard: six decodes split four to two for 'nothing happens to me' over 'nothing happens to Maria', and a human listener played 00:01:55-00:02:26 and reports 'nothing's going to happen to Maria in the meantime'. That report is recorded as its own provisional target, and it is primed - the listener knew the hypothesis before listening, which is exactly the weakness B04 was told to preserve rather than launder. Read together: the ear now favours Maria, the machines favour me, and the corpus records both with their conditions instead of picking. An earlier version of this note said a human ear did not settle it and cited a report of the neighbouring 00:02:05 line; that report stands and is in the Pulse-and-Kat item, and this is a second, later listening over a wider span. Why the item is kept has not changed: it tests whether a decoder's contextual prior can manufacture a name in a campaign saturated with it. The 'Tower Play' framing is a second metadata trap - the group plans the tower run here and reaches the tower later in the episode.

selection.diagnostic_value: The only real audio in the corpus with a verified fetch and a listened-through truth section. In ten minutes it exercises music over speech, a recap that states prior-session events inside the window, an explicit player-to-character mapping spoken aloud, a relayed in-fiction phone call, Shadowrun vocabulary that both reference decoders got wrong, and a named entity that the episode title supplies but the audio does not.
risks: Truth is machine-assisted, not human-verified by ear. Every engine that touched it is listed in truth.contaminating_providers - five of them, two used for the window decodes and three consulted on contested passages - and each carries an undeclared advantage when scored against this truth; see the notes file before reporting a score.

Diarization can be probed here but not scored precisely: one mixed 16 kHz track with no per-speaker channel, seven speaking roles heard, and only two distinct people demonstrated. The gap between 7 and 2 is evidence this recording does not supply, not a range to average over.
It is an online podcast with post-production levelling and gating, not the target single-room iPad condition, and the corpus still lacks that tier.
The publisher serves the file from its own host; link rot or a re-encode would invalidate every anchor recorded here, which is why the digest is recorded and checked rather than assumed.
